item.title: Hot Picks: Three U.S. financial stocks with earnings growth potential
item.description: Keith Buchanan shares his views on Travelers, Aflac and Wells Fargo and the earnings potential of U.S. financial stocks.
item.dc:creator: BNN Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: The U.S. financial sector offers a window into business activity and consumer finances. Trading, initial public offerings, advisory work and credit trends help reveal the economy’s health. BNN Bloomberg spoke with Keith Buchanan, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments, about his three financial stock selections and how he evaluates opportunities across banking and insurance. Key Takeaways Read the full transcript below: LINDSAY: It’s time now for Hot Picks, and our next guest has three financial companies on his radar. Let’s welcome in Keith Buchanan, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments. Great to have you join us once again. Thank you. KEITH: Thank you. LINDSAY: So, before we get into your actual picks, I always like to start with a broader look at the financial—at the sector. And this—today we’re talking about financials. What do you think is driving the financial sector right now? Is it one thing? Is it interest rates, earnings growth, the broader economy? Is it a number of things? KEITH: I choose all the above. I think the financials is a unique space that really gives a glimpse into the window of many facets for our economy. We’ve seen interest rate volatility, trading, some anxiety among investors, also the IPO movement, and also the advisory businesses all really come together to kind of give a glimpse of business America and how small and midsize business are performing, but also some of the consumer elements, too, with credit cards and that, you know, some of the credit issues that—that are starting to bubble up here at the larger banks. We get a full view of—of the broader economy, which is interesting in covering the group on a day-to-day basis. LINDSAY: Okay, so let’s get into your picks, then. The first one is Travelers. I know this—this company just also reported earnings. So tell us more about the opportunities you see—you see right now. KEITH: Sure, Travelers is a company that really just is executing in a very high clip, not only from a, you know, writing profitable business, but also investment portfolios kicking in extra earnings that kind of just put the ice meal on the cake. The insurance business right now is one that—that gets left behind in moments like we’ve seen over the last couple of years. But in moments like we are right now, where there are several risks that investors are becoming more and more concerned about, the market really looks at some of these names as a very stable provider of earnings, which we think earnings will be kind of the balance of whether this market holds up over the next 12 to 18 months or whether there’s a bear market that ensues. And names like this will be more attractive the more the latter becomes a fear of the broader market. So Travelers is a name that we really feel like offers a lot to our clients’ portfolios right now. LINDSAY: And it delivered a really strong third quarter. Like, what do you think was behind that performance? KEITH: Again, just growing a profitable business. They—they’ve been able to move in P&C and property and casualty in a way that most smaller corporations haven’t been able to. They’re broader geographically, so they have been able to diversify from a lot of just really concentrated risks, whether it’s weather-related or otherwise. So, being bigger has been better, and they’ve been able to really execute it on an underwriting standpoint. LINDSAY: Okay, Aflac, your next company for today, your next pick. Tell us more about this one. KEITH: Sure, Aflac is a little different from Travelers. It doesn’t have, like, the best-of-breed allure to it. It has a, you know, of course, a big part of its business is in Japan, so we have to understand how currency really affects from a couple of different standpoints. But they’ve been executing a really more of a self-help story within the insurance space, smaller and, of course, you know, a different facet of the business. But, you know, Aflac has been able to perform extremely well from a stock standpoint, and we’re really—again, it really—we really appreciate what it offers our strategy going forward. For specifically within the financial space, where it’s really hard to find these more stable earnings growers without concerns about the economy declines over the next couple of years. LINDSAY: Well, because Japan is one of Aflac’s biggest markets, right? Like, are they facing any pressure from the rising interest rates and a weaker yen? KEITH: Yes, they are, but in an interesting, kind of ironic way, the fear that kind of comes up from that actually drives, from a pricing standpoint, better pricing environment in Japan. So that—that’s kind of helped them in a—in a really ironic twist of fate. So we really, from aspect of what it offers their business lines, you know, exposure to Japan is something we actually become to enjoy in these—again, some of these moments where we have a little more fear permeating the marketplace. LINDSAY: Okay, your last pick for today is Wells Fargo. Tell us more about that. KEITH: Again, another self-help story, but more on the major bank side. Without the asset cap now, they really have opened the door, and execution is the way they kind of drive value through that door. You get it at a discount that, frankly, has been warranted over the last several years. We feel like it might be a way to really drive shareholder value going forward. The earnings picture is much more clear now, and we feel like Wells has a diversification among its businesses and its geographies in order to drive that value going forward and close that valuation gap between Wells Fargo and the rest of the major banks. We feel like it’s a self-help story that’s earnings-driven and really has upside from here. LINDSAY: I just want to go back to the general sector as well. Like, what’s the biggest risk—risk do you think financial stocks maybe face over the next even year or so? KEITH: Sure. The biggest risk is a flattening yield curve that is—brings along the economic strain that a more distressed economy, even a recession, is among the more likely options. That’s not really baked in right now, but with the banks having so much market cap, the insurers and those names believe are having a market cap to continue to drive the space higher. That is the scenario that we’re going to in the 20—later 2027, maybe even 2028. So economic decline is obviously the risk there, and also, you know, a more flattening yield curve makes that—that book of business or the big banks and traditional lending business much more difficult to become profitable. So those are the concerns we have with the space going forward. LINDSAY: Okay, we got to leave it there. Keith Buchanan, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments. Great to have you join us. Thank you. --- This BNN Bloomberg summary and transcript of the Oct. 22, 2026 interview with Keith Buchanan are published with the assistance of AI. item.title: Canadian agriculture’s $12 billion opportunity
item.description: Canada’s agriculture industry has an opportunity to unlock billions of dollars in revenue from new markets and customers as it adjusts to a reimagined trading relationship with the U.S., says the head ...
item.dc:creator: Jordan Fleguel
item.content:encoded: Canada’s agriculture industry has an opportunity to unlock billions of dollars in revenue from new markets and customers as it adjusts to a reimagined trading relationship with the U.S., says the head of Farm Credit Canada (FCC). “We see an opportunity in terms of diversification of markets, and that opportunity has been quantified,” Justine Hendricks, president and CEO of FCC, told BNN Bloomberg on Thursday. “If you take a look over and above the north-south trade, which we know and recognize is important to this industry, there is a $12 billion opportunity that overall is there for us to go and get.” As a federal Crown corporation, FCC provides financing and advisory services to the agriculture industry, and reports to Canadians and Parliament through Canada’s Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food. Hendricks noted that many Canadian agriculture products can still flow into the U.S. tariff free but given the current uncertain and sometimes hostile relationship between Ottawa and Washington, the sector should be looking to diversify its customer base. “So, there are some levers that the industry can lean on to also help navigate and frankly increase its diversification, which is an important tool as part of your risk mitigation,” she said. Her comments came amid ongoing trade tensions between Canada and the U.S., one of a number of factors creating uncertainty for Canadian farmers. Another is the cost of diesel fuel, which has reached historically high levels in recent months, shrinking Canadian farmers’ already-tight margins, as laid out in an FCC report released Wednesday. “It’s not just diesel prices, right, there’s what’s going on with the U.S., climate is also a key factor, (as is) the overall cost of input,” said Hendricks. “All of these elements have impact, and as a result of it, the environment that farmers and producers have to navigate has just become increasingly more complex.” Industry resilience Hendricks said the good news is that Canadian farmers, ranchers and producers are known for their agility and resilience in the face of uncertainty and change. “And we’ve got evidence to show – from the growth of the industry, to what it continues to provide as gross domestic product (GDP) to Canada – that it is continuing to thrive despite some of this complexity,” she said. Last year, Canada’s agriculture and agri-food industry generated $158 billion, or around seven per cent, of Canada’s total GDP, according to government figures. The sector employed approximately 2.3 million people in 2025, accounting for one in nine jobs across the country. In addition to diversifying its market access, Canadian agriculture should be focusing on increasing investment in innovation to drive growth going forward, Hendricks argued, noting that Canada lags behind many of its peers in that area. “That is one of the reasons why 18 months ago FCC stood up a capital division to respond directly to that gap,” she said, adding that since the division was launched, FCC has deployed over half a billion dollars towards funding innovation in Canadian food and agriculture. “We do feel that there is capital available, and certainly FCC has a role to play there, and that is why we’ve stood up and put our money where our mouth is so to speak to be able to play an active role and we’re starting to see some results.”

item.title: Tesla drops as spending pullback clouds AI, robotics ambitions
item.description: Tesla’s shares slid five per cent in premarket trading on Thursday as the EV maker’s reduced capital spending forecast raised questions about the pace of investment behind Elon Musk’s AI, robotics and ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: Tesla’s shares slid five per cent in premarket trading on Thursday as the EV maker’s reduced capital spending forecast raised questions about the pace of investment behind Elon Musk’s AI, robotics and autonomous-driving ambitions. The company on Wednesday lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast to about US$20 billion from more than $25 billion after spending far less than expected on AI and robotics in the third quarter, which led to a surprise positive free cash flow. The strong position may prove valuable as CEO Musk explores combining Tesla with the far more capital-intensive SpaceX. But “investors are likely to come away with mixed feelings,” J.P.Morgan analysts, led by Rajat Gupta, wrote in a note. “The delay helps near-term cash burn but also suggests delays in investments that matter for fruition of long-term opportunities.” Wednesday’s management commentary suggested spending will be ramped up in 2027 and 2028 as Tesla continues to fund robotaxi, Optimus, AI compute and Terafab milestones, the brokerage said. Tesla’s shares have declined about 14 per cent this year, in contrast to the Nasdaq’s roughly 15 per cent gain. The stock is about 23 per cent below its record intraday high of $498.83, reached in December 2025. Its valuation, however, remains well above peers: Tesla traded at 188.24 times its forward earnings estimates, compared with 6.58 for Ford and 5.16 for General Motors. “The risk is Tesla now enters a period of limbo while investors await news on a potential combination with SpaceX, which ... might face significant regulatory hurdles,” said Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell. (Reporting by Joel Jose in Bengaluru; Editing by Joyjeet Das)

item.title: Melanie Paradis: Streamlining mines is good, but Ottawa needs a plan to finance them
item.description: Political analyst and communications expert Melanie Paradis warns that the federal government’s new fast-track regulatory bill will not be enough to spark a new resources boom, unless Ottawa actively ...
item.content:encoded:
Melanie Paradis is the president of Texture Communications and has worked at the intersection of mining and politics for 20 years. There is a tendency in Ottawa to think that if you permit a mine, the capital will flow. But those working in the mining industry and on Bay Street know it isn’t that simple.

This week, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said the world is entering the “largest investment supercycle in the history of the metals and mining industry.” A supercycle refers to a long period of investment in new mines driven by significant shifts in the global economy. According to Hodgson, this supercycle is tied to increased demand for critical minerals generated by changes to the industrial strategies and economic policies of many countries. To leverage this, the federal government introduced Bill C-39 , the Building Canada Strong Act , to compress into one year a federal approvals process that routinely takes several. But while government policy decides which projects are permitted, prices decide which ones get built. When the two line up, Canada builds mines. When they don’t, no amount of legislative reform fills the gap. To actually build Canada strong, C-39 must be the first step in a countercyclical industrial strategy for mining that would accelerate viable projects today, build the infrastructure tomorrow’s mines will need, and work with allies to make strategically important minerals financeable even when markets are manipulated. Let’s start with the last time a government bet on regulatory reform. In 2012, Stephen Harper’s government overhauled federal environmental assessments to speed up resource development, just as the last commodity supercycle was ending. Mineral exploration spending in Canada fell from about $4.2 billion in 2011 to $1.6 billion in 2016. The new rules were designed to be faster, but the regulatory reform alone could not reverse the collapse in investment. The capital hurdle Today’s federal government must learn from that experience that while C-39 can make a mine permittable, it can’t attract investors to the mine with a permit alone. The reverse is also true. Government would also be wise not to spurn financeable mines with an overly narrow definition of “national interest.” Gold is a good example. According to the Scotia Growth Institute , gold now accounts for 46 per cent of the value of Canada’s 10 largest mining commodities, up from just 24 per cent three years ago. Gold projects have and will continue to advance in response to market demand, and for that reason they tend to fly under the notice of governments. But treating gold as an afterthought because it doesn’t fit the critical minerals narrative would be a mistake. A gold mine that opens in 2028 trains a workforce and builds the roads and power lines that the next critical-minerals project will be able to leverage. It also proves to investors that Canada can take a deposit from discovery to production. When prices for other commodities recover, that track record will let Canadian critical minerals projects raise capital quickly. It’s therefore in the national interest for viable mines that don’t meet the definition of “critical minerals,” like gold, to be opened. Beijing’s market chokehold Some critical minerals are not as easily financed in the current market, and many of Canada’s biggest deposits sit in feasibility purgatory despite the government’s desire to see them advance. And this is not by accident. Beijing floods the market to drive down prices, which starves Western projects of capital so they don’t get built, securing China’s grip on vital supply chains. A U.S. congressional select committee has documented this predatory pricing, and Washington is now pursuing agreements to establish a trade zone for critical minerals with tariffs and price floors to help build supply chains within allied countries. Because of ongoing trade negotiations with the U.S., Canada has not yet committed to that plan. The job of government is to invest in readiness during the lean years so that when prices align, projects are permitted, financed and ready to build. C-39 offers a tool for that. Its proposed Regions of National Interest could streamline federal approvals inside a designated mining district, for example. The time to designate those regions with provinces and Indigenous partners is now; we should build the roads and power lines that will make future mines less expensive to develop. Laying that foundation also means treating the national-interest list as a floor, not a ceiling. The projects on the list deserve the attention they’re getting, but the same speed should be available to every viable mine. And where the government invests its own money, it should strategically serve as a counterweight to market manipulation. Taken together, these steps would form the foundation of a countercyclical industrial strategy for mining to ensure we are ready for the mining supercycle, Hodgson says, is just beginning.
